name: Likango, langue des Bakango
confidence_why: The only description of Kango accent is a single passing remark in Calonne-Beaufaict 1912, a colonial administrator's sociological notes rather than a grammar, saying that word-final syllables are unaccented in ordinary speech and take a secondary accent only when shouted across the river, while Hutereau 1910 and Védy 1906 say nothing about accent at all, so neither the place of main stress nor whether Kango has stress or tone is established.
catalog_citation: Calonne-Beaufaict, Adolphe de. 1912. Études Bakango: notes de sociologie coloniale. Liège: Mathieu Thone. 152 pp. (archive.org tudesbakangonote00calo; HathiTrust uc1.$b750030)
catalog_locator: Chapter 'II. — La langue likango' (pp. 31-35): p. 34, sentence beginning 'Envisageons les conditions spéciales', continuing to p. 35; and p. 32, paragraph c). Annex 'Quelques mots Likango' pp. 133-138.
catalog_quote: [p. 32] J'ai indiqué dans mon étude du libwâlé qu'il était probable que bon nombre de mots avaient perdu, par l'usage, des syllabes finales non accentuées, syllabes qui devaient exister en vieux libwâlé. Dans la langue likango, nous trouvons une confirmation de cette hypothèse; ces syllabes ont été conservées ... [p. 34] Envisageons les conditions spéciales d'utilisation du likango, parlé par une population vivant la majeure partie de l'année sur les rochers, et engageant d'interminables causeries à longue distance, ce qui oblige de faire porter sur les syllabes finales non accentuées un accent secondaire qu'on ne trouve pas dans la conversation normale. La question se pose de savoir si la conservation de ces syllabes finales n'est pas due précisément à cette nécessité de se faire entendre au loin.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: Consider the special conditions in which Likango is used: it is spoken by a population that lives on the rocks for most of the year and carries on interminable conversations over long distances, which forces a secondary accent to be placed on the unaccented final syllables, an accent not found in normal conversation. The question arises whether the preservation of these final syllables is not due precisely to this need to make oneself heard from afar.
new_statements.citation: Calonne-Beaufaict, Adolphe de. 1912. Études Bakango: notes de sociologie coloniale. Liège: Mathieu Thone.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 'II. — La langue likango', p. 34 (continues to p. 35; pp. 42-43); cf. p. 32 (p. 40) 'syllabes finales non accentuées'
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (174 PDF pages, text present; extracted text, no scanned needed). The quoted passage is on printed p. 34 = p. 42, chapter "II. — La langue likango" (pp. 39-43 = printed pp. 31-35), verbatim apart from line-break hyphenation ("dis-tance", "con-versation", "conser-vation"): "Envisageons les conditions spéciales d'utilisation du likango, parlé par une population vivant la majeure partie de l'année sur les rochers, et engageant d'interminables causeries à longue distance, ce qui oblige de faire porter sur les syllabes finales non accentuées un accent secondaire qu'on ne trouve pas dans la conversation normale. La question se pose de savoir si la conservation de ces syllabes finales n'est…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The author treats word-final syllables as unaccented in ordinary speech (so the accent is non-final), but never says which syllable carries the accent; penultimate would be the Bantu default but the source does not state it. In long-distance calling across the river a secondary accent is added on the final syllable. This is a passing remark in a colonial ethnography, not a phonological description, and says nothing about tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A 'secondary accent' on final syllables only in long-distance shouting; explicitly absent in normal conversation.
new_statements.exceptions: None. p. 32 adds, for the related Libwale (Bwa) dialect, that many words lost 'syllabes finales non accentuées' which Likango has.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('mots', 'syllabes finales'); contrast is ordinary conversation vs long-distance calling. Data are cited words in a comparative vocabulary with vowel-quality diacritics only; no stress or tone marking.
new_statements.identity_note: Calonne-Beaufaict 1912 describes 'le likango', the language of the Bakango fishermen of the Uele river (Bondo-Bima stretch), which he calls 'un dialecte ababua' closer to Libati (western Bwa) than to Libwale; Glottolog maps the book to kty (kang1286) and classifies Kango separately from Bwa (bwaa1238, bww) under Late Bomokandian. The ISP Buta theses concern the Bambesa variety ('Lekango = Kango de Bambesa'), Bakuye 2011 the Poko variety. Do not confuse with Kango (Tshopo District) [kzy, kang1285], the Bantu-speaking pygmy group of the Ituri described by Schebesta; those Glottolog 'Bakango' references are not this language.

tone_statements.citation: Kujath, Elizabeth & Matthew Faytak. 2026. Phonetic characteristics of two series of high vowels in Kango. In: Bantu11 - 11th International Conference on Bantu Languages, Ghent University, 18-21 : Book of Abstracts (version 2026-08-13), pp. 130-131. Ghent: UGent Centre for Bantu Studies (BantUGent).
tone_statements.quote: Methods. Data for the study was collected in Bambesa (Bas-Uélé province, DRC) in summer 2024. Ten participants (5M, 5F, mean age 54, SD 13.8) provided data from elicitation sessions in French, Lingala, and/or Kango (per speaker preference). Sessions were recorded on a Marantz PMD561 solid-state recorder using the internal microphone. Stimuli featured the target vowels in the first stem syllable with a preference for H tone on the target.

sources.note: No phonology section; the language chapter is a comparative vocabulary of Likango vs the Ababua (Bwa) dialects Libati and Libwale. Two remarks on accent: p. 32 speaks of 'syllabes finales non accentuées' lost in old Libwale but preserved in Likango; p. 34 says that in normal conversation final syllables are unaccented and that long-distance river talk forces a secondary accent onto them. The position of the primary accent is never stated; word forms carry only vowel-quality diacritics (è, é, ô), not stress marks. No tone information.

sources.note: Accurately characterised by S2: a two-page conference abstract (acoustics of two series of high vowels), not a tone description. Its only tonal content is (i) the methods sentence that stimuli were chosen 'with a preference for H tone on the target' (first stem syllable), which presupposes a lexical H tone category in Kango, and (ii) acute-marked vs unmarked syllables in the Table 1 citation forms (ɓísu̧, púsu, ɛsesé, míso, lisɛ́kɛ́, sɔpɔ́, kása vs mosi, mosi̧). No inventory, TBU, contour, downstep or rule statement; 'tonal-unspecified' is the right coding and the row should be filed as margi…

tone.quote: There are a number of words that have a root-medial [k] in the western dialects of Pagibete (Mongwapele and Omveda) and in Kango, but no [k] in the other Pagibete dialect or in the Bwa Cluster. [...] If the (eastern) Pagibete/Kango [k] is between like vowels, these vowels coalesce in the other Bwa Bloc dialects. Of the six best examples, four have [´Ñkò] in Pagibete east corresponding to [ˆÑ] in the other dialects. Note that not only do the vowels coalesce, leaving a single-length vowel, but so do the high and low tones, leaving a falling tone. There is no vowel or tone coalescence in the other cases.
tone.locator: Section 2.4.1 'Phonetic' (Linguistic Findings), p. 32, paragraph introducing Table 5 'Correspondences [k] versus no [k]'; cf. Table 4b note p. 31; Appendix H, Matrix 5
